title: Stories about poems
translation: Someone tells you the story behind a poem, and the poem turns out to be bad. What a letdown. Anyone who knew even a little about poetry wouldn't tell it as if it were something special.
In general, when people go on about things they know nothing about, it's embarrassing just to listen.
original: {人|ひと}のかたり{出|い}でたる{歌物語|うたものがたり}の、{歌|うた}のわろきこそ{本意|ほい}なけれ。
すこしその{道|みち}{知|し}らむ{人|ひと}は、いみじと{思|おも}ひては{語|かた}らじ。
すべていとも{知|し}らぬ{道|みち}の{物|もの}がたりしたる、かたはらいたく{聞|き}きにくし。
literal: When, in a poem story that someone tells, the poem is bad: that is disappointing.
A person who knows that way even a little would not tell it thinking it splendid.
In general, (people) telling stories about a way they know nothing at all about is embarrassing and unpleasant to hear.

notes.text: {歌物語|うたものがたり}: here, a story about how a poem came to be written: who wrote it, for whom, and what happened. (The same word is also the name of a genre, tales built around poems, such as the Tales of Ise.) The story only works if the poem at its centre is good.

notes.quote: 歌のわろきこそ本意なけれ
notes.text: こそ … けれ. {本意|ほい}なし: 'disappointing, not what one hoped for'. The same word closes a sentence in section 1 (本意なきわざなれ, 'what a waste').
{道|みち}: here, the art of poetry. む in an attributive position: 'a person who might know', 'anyone who knows'.
じ: the negative of む, 'would not'. Someone who knows poetry would see the poem is bad and keep quiet.

かたはらいたし: 'embarrassing to watch', literally 'painful to be beside'. The 1925 edition: you feel sorry for them even watching from the side. Modern {片腹痛|かたはらいた}い (with the kanji for 'one side of the belly') means 'laughable, ridiculous'.
